claims.text: The as-synthesized platinum-group-metal high-entropy nanoscale catalyst has a disordered surface structure.
The catalyst's disordered surface contains heterogeneous local electronic environments.
Post-synthesis thermal annealing under an inert atmosphere will increase atomic ordering of the platinum-group-metal sites.
Increased surface atomic ordering alters the local electronic structure, including the distribution of d-band centers.
The local electronic structure tunes the adsorption energies of ethanol and its oxidation intermediates.
Multiple platinum-group-metal configurations in the disordered catalyst create a range of active sites.
The heterogeneous active sites act synergistically to adjust the binding strengths of ethanol and its oxidation intermediates.
The adjusted binding strengths facilitate complete 12-electron oxidation of ethanol.
Annealing-induced atomic ordering reduces the beneficial heterogeneity of active sites.
Reduced active-site heterogeneity produces less-optimal adsorption energies.
Less-optimal adsorption energies decrease ethanol-oxidation catalytic activity.
Less-optimal adsorption energies may shift ethanol-oxidation selectivity.
The annealed catalyst will have lower ethanol-oxidation current density than the as-synthesized catalyst.
The annealed catalyst will have lower ethanol-oxidation mass activity than the as-synthesized catalyst.
Annealing may change the ethanol-oxidation product distribution and diminish complete 12-electron oxidation.
The proposed disorder-performance relationship applies under alkaline, moderate-temperature fuel-cell operating conditions.
Changes in pH, temperature, or reaction environment may alter the role of atomic disorder.
Similar or improved activity and complete-oxidation selectivity in the more ordered catalyst would falsify the proposed necessity of disorder-induced synergy.
